narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 53.4% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly above a coin flip, but under an admissions rule that treats predicted failure as disqualifying, it was enough to reject your application.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing. Being in the lowest decile, compared with accepted students who averaged around the middle of their class, pushed the prediction toward failure more than any other item. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most influential factor. At 3.40, it is above the accepted-student average of 3.23, so it worked in your favor and pushed toward passing. Your upper-middle family-income background was the third factor and modestly favored passing rather than failure relative to the applicant group. In short, the denial was driven mainly by weak third-year class rank; your GPA and family background helped offset that concern but not enough to move the estimate below the rejection threshold.

To strengthen a future application, focus on evidence that directly addresses bar-exam risk: improve performance in advanced law coursework, begin structured bar preparation and diagnostic practice early, and consider submitting updated grades or a brief explanation of any circumstances behind your third-year standing. A stronger third-year class rank would likely change this prediction most.
